words.note: Literally "victory": the everyday hello, any time of day.
The usual answer to გამარჯობა.
The polite form, for strangers, older people and in shops.
Everyday yes.
"You" for one person you know well.
After a number the noun stays singular: ორი ჩაი, "two tea".

example.en: There are seven days in a week.
There are twelve months in a year.

words.note: Georgian counts in twenties: 30 is "twenty and ten", 40 is "two twenties".
ოც-და-ათი: twenty and ten.
ორ-მ-ოცი: two twenties.

example.en: The milk is in the fridge.

words.note: Bread baked with cheese, Georgia's best-known dish.
Twisted dumplings filled with meat and broth, eaten by hand.

example.en: Fruit is cheap at the market.
The plane is in the sky.
The car is parked behind the house.
The pharmacy is next to the bank.

words.note: Georgia's money. One lari is 100 tetri (თეთრი).
Careful: დედა is mother and მამა is father.
და also means "and".

example.en: The room is big and bright.
The book is on the table.
The glass is on the table.
Yesterday I was at the market.
I'll be back in a week.

words.note: კვირა means both "week" and "Sunday".

example.en: I'll be in Tbilisi for a month.
In the morning I drink coffee.
In the evening I'm at home.

words.note: Days from Monday: ორშაბათი, სამშაბათი, ოთხშაბათი, ხუთშაბათი — "two, three, four, five after Saturday".

example.en: On Friday we're going to the cinema.
On Saturday I go to the market.
— The menu, please. — Here you are.
— What do you recommend? — The khinkali.
— What would you like? — I want water.
— The bill, please. — Just a moment.

words.note: Said with a raised glass, like "cheers".

example.en: — How much is this? — Three lari.

example.ka: — ერთი კილო ვაშლი, თუ შეიძლება. — აი, ინებეთ.
example.lat: — erti k'ilo vashli, tu sheidzleba. — ai, inebet.
example.en: — A kilo of apples, please. — Here you are.

example.ka: ეს ძალიან ძვირია, უფრო იაფი გაქვთ?
example.lat: es dzalian dzviria, upro iapi gakvt?
example.en: This is very expensive, do you have a cheaper one?

example.ka: — ბარათით შეიძლება? — კი, რა თქმა უნდა.
example.lat: — baratit sheidzleba? — k'i, ra tkma unda.
example.en: — Can I pay by card? — Yes, of course.
Excuse me, I need a bag.

example.ka: — კიდევ რამე? — არა, სულ ეს არის.
example.lat: — k'idev rame? — ara, sul es aris.

example.en: — Where are you going? — To the airport, please.
— How much to the centre? — Ten lari.
Slowly, please, I have a child with me.
— Is it far? — No, it's near.
Excuse me, where is the metro?
Turn left at the end of the street.
Hello, Mrs Nana, how are you?
— How are you? — Fine, and you?
— I'm Nana. — Very nice to meet you.
I've had a headache since the morning.
The child has a stomach ache.
I've had a fever since yesterday.
Excuse me, where is the pharmacy?
— Where do you work? — At a bank.
I work in an office, in the centre.
I have a meeting at ten.
Just a moment, I'm coming right away.
It's hot today, let's go to the sea!
It's cold today, put on a hat.
I really like Georgia, the people are warm.
Tbilisi is a beautiful city, especially in the evening.

words.note: Georgian has no he/she: ის is used for both, and for things.
Use თქვენ for several people, and politely for one person.
Often shortened to -ა on the end of a word: სახლშია, "is at home".

example.en: How many children do you have?

words.note: Goes right before the verb.
თუ შეიძლება, "if it's possible", is how you say please.
"Not able to": put it before the verb instead of არ.
